sentences.text: JUDGMENT

This suit is filed by the plaintiffs against defendants for an order of permanent prohibitory injunction restraining the defendants No.1 & 2 from disturbing the plaintiffs' peaceful possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule house or any other house in which they reside or occupy in future.

2. The case of the plaintiffs in brief is as hereunder:-
The plaintiffs No.1 & 2 are husband and wife.
Defendant No.1 is their son and defendant No.2 is the wife of defendant No.1.
The suit schedule premises is a tenanted house premise availed in the name of plaintiff No.2 and they are residing along with their 2nd son Akash Shendge.

Initially during the lock down period the defendant No.2 came to the house of the plaintiffs along with the defendant No.1 as a friend and thereafter they have married and wherein residing in the house of the plaintiffs.
After the marriage, there was disharmony between defendant No.1 & 2 which has led to filing of a petition for judicial separation in MC No.5699/2023 which was later compromised and withdrawn.
As per the advise of the plaintiffs and other well wishers, defendant No.2 moved out of the plaintiffs' house and started to live in a shared accommodation with her friend.

Though the plaintiffs have insisted the defendant No.1 to set up a separate house and live separately with his wife as there was paucity of accommodation in their house the defendants started to continue living in their house.
There was serious matrimonial differences between defendant No.1 and 2 and complaints were also lodged before the Police by the defendant No.2 against the plaintiffs.
Subsequently the defendant No.1 has filed MC.No.5699/2023 for dissolution of the marriage which is pending before the Family Court.
The defendant No.2 is very abusive, created ruckus and destroyed the peace in the house.

She used to go out and shout as "help me" and would also tell that she was being troubled by the plaintiffs in order to attract the attention of the neighbours and public.
She has also threatened that she would commit suicide.
Though a complaint was lodged, the Police have refused to intervene and insisted to approach the Family Court.
The plaintiff No.1 has suffered chest pain due to the stress and the defendants are insensitive, cruel and cunning.

Since they are creating ruckus in the house, the plaintiffs have filed this suit to direct the defendants to vacate the suit schedule house and to restrain them from entering the house and thereby prevent them from disturbing their peaceful enjoyment of their life.
3. Pursuant to the suit summons issued by this Court, both the defendants entered appearance and filed their separate written statement.

In the written statement filed by the defendant No.1, he has admitted the relationship of the parties and the matrimonial dispute and MC cases filed by him for judicial separation and subsequently for divorce.
It is contended by him that defendant No.2 is very much adamant, dominating, suspicious and fighting with him.
It is stated that later defendant No.2 moved out of his parental house and living in a shared accommodation with her friend.

It is also stated that defendant No.2 has developed animosity towards his parents and defendant No.2 is living separately with her friend and he is also living separately in a paying guest accommodation.
It is also contended that defendant No.2 is well educated and she is having a lucrative job and earning well.

4. In the written statement filed by the defendant No.2, while admitting the relationship and marriage, she has contended that even prior to the marriage she was residing in the plaintiff's house and the plaintiffs have also taught the customs and rituals followed at their house and subsequently the plaintiffs began to turn hostile and therefore defendants have registered their marriage in the presence of friends on 30.11.2020.
It is also stated that after the marriage also they have resided together in the plaintiffs' house wherein she was harassed by the plaintiffs.

It is her contention that when her aged mother fell sick and succumbed to death on 26.10.2023 she rushed to her home town to perform her last rites and taking the advantage of her absence the plaintiffs have filed this suit and succeeded in getting exparte temporary injunction.
It is contended by her that defendant No.1 is residing in the plaintiffs' house and she has a legal right to reside in the house of the plaintiffs along with the defendant No.1.
On these grounds she has sought for dismissal of the suit.

5. On the basis of the above pleadings this Court has framed the following issues:-
1) Whether the plaintiffs prove that defendants have committed domestic violence against the plaintiff No.2?
2) Whether the defendant No.2 proves that the plaintiffs have committed domestic violence against her?

The relationship of the parties is not in dispute.

It is also not in dispute that the plaintiffs are residing in a rented flat as tenants having availed the premises under rent agreement dated 04.09.2018 executed in favour of the plaintiff No.2 Shantha Shendge.
It is also not in dispute that prior to the marriage, itself the plaintiffs and defendant No.1 have permitted the defendant No.2 to reside in the suit schedule house.

It is also not in dispute that on 30.11.2020 the defendants 1 & 2 married under Special Marriage Act without informing the plaintiffs and later the came to the house of the plaintiffs and during post marriage also they were residing with the plaintiffs.

10. According to the plaintiffs, the defendant No.2 is abusive, insensitive, cruel and unnecessarily created ruckus and destroyed their peaceful life, used to go out of the house and shout, "help me"
and would also tell that she is being troubled by the plaintiffs in order to attract the attention of the neighbours and public and thereby totally disturbed their peace in the evening of their life.

It is also stated that the defendant No.2 was threatening to commit suicide and thereby the plaintiff No.1 who is the senior citizen has suffered chest pain and hence sought an order of permanent injunction against the defendants No.1 & 2 restraining them from disturbing the peaceful enjoyment of the suit schedule property.
The defendant No.1 is the son of the plaintiffs.
He has almost supported the case of the plaintiffs.

The defendant No.2 has contended that even prior to the marriage when she was residing along with the plaintiffs in the suit schedule house, though she was taught customs and Suresh Kumar vs Chandan Shendge on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180413825/
4 rituals followed in their house, the plaintiff No.2 raised issues when the defendant No.2 was unable to head bath every time which has constantly affected her health and they were not prepared to perform the marriage and therefore ultimately they have registered their marriage in the presence of their friends.

It is further contended that the plaintiffs were not ready to accept the marriage and after the marriage, during her stay she was constantly abused, threated, harassed to a large extent and the plaintiffs have intervened the marital relationship of the defendants.
She has specifically pleaded that she has a right to reside in the matrimonial home .
It is her contention that her mother fell sick and died on 26.10.2023 and when she rushed to her home town taking advantage of her absence, the plaintiffs have filed this suit.
Her defence is that she has a shared house hold right over the suit schedule house and hence, she cannot be excluded by way of injunction.
11. The plaintiffs being the father-in-law and mother-in-law of the defendant No.2 sought an order of injunction against defendant No.2 alleging harassment by the defendant No.2.

In the mean time,
though the defendant No.2 has not specifically invoked the provisions of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 pleaded that the suit schedule house is her shared house hold and the plaintiffs have committed domestic violence and she has a right to reside in it.

sentences.text: Therefore a question arose before the court as to whether a suit filed by the parents-in- law of an aggrieved person for injunction is maintainable when the daughter in law has resisted the suit alleging domestic violence on the part of the plaintiffs.

This issue is elaborately dealt by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Satish Chander Ahuja v/s Sneha Ahuja in (2021)1 Supreme Court Cases 414 wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has clearly held that in a case of this nature the suit filed by the parents is maintainable and in the same time in the very same suit when the daughter in law alleges domestic violence and claims the house as a shared household to have a right to reside in it, the civil court must consider it by virtue of Section 26 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 even if no separate application is made by daughter in law.

entities.text: Satish Chander Ahuja v/s Sneha Ahuja in (2021)1 Supreme Court Cases 414
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has further held that the right of residence provided u/s 19 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 is not the indefeasible right of residence to an aggrieved daughter in law especially when the daughter in law is pitted against father-in-law and mother-in-law in a suit.

entities.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has further held that senior citizens at their advanced age are entitled to live peacefully not haunted by marital discord between their son and daughter in law.

The specific portion of the observation made by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the aforesaid decision is extracted for ready reference:-
Para-100 "

As per Section 26, any relief available under Sections 18, 19, 20, 21 and 22 of the 2005 Act may also be sought in any legal proceeding, before a civil court,
family court or a criminal court being the aggrieved person.
Thus, the defendant is entitled to claim relief under Section 19 in suit, which has been filed by the plaintiff.
Section 26 empowers the aggrieved person to claim above relief in civil courts also.
In the present suit, it was the defence of the defendant that the house being the shared household, she is entitled to reside in the house as per Section 17(1) of the 2005 Act".
Para-103- "This Court held that Section 26 has to be interpreted in a manner to effectuate the purpose and object of the Act.

This Court held that the determination of claim of the aggrieved person was necessary in the suit to avoid multiplicity of Suresh Kumar vs Chandan Shendge on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180413825/
5 proceedings.
This Court laid down the following in paras 40 and 41 (Vaishali Abhimanyu Joshi Case, SCC pp.388-89)".

Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court to balance the rights of the parties in para-90 held as under:-
" Before we close our discussion on Section 2(s), we need to observe that the right to residence under Section 19 is not an indefeasible right of residence in shared household especially when the daughter-in-law is pitted against aged father-in-law and mother-in-law.
The senior citizens in the evening of their life are also entitled to live peacefully not haunted by marital discord between their son and daughter-in-law.
While granting relief both in application under Section 12 of the DV Act, 2005 or in any civil proceedings, the court has to balance the rights of both the parties.
The directions issued by the High Court adequately balances the rights of both the parties".

Further the Hon'ble Supreme Court in para-124 has held that- "Drawing the analogy from the above case, we are of the opinion that the expression "save in accordance with the procedure established by law", in Section 17(2) of the 2005 Act contemplates the proceedings in the court of competent jurisdiction.

Thus,
suit for mandatory and permanent injunction/eviction or possession by the owner of the property is maintainable before a competent court.
We may further notice that in sub-section (2) the injunction is "shall not be evicted or excluded from the shared household... save in accordance with procedure established by law".
Thus, the provision itself contemplates adopting of any procedure established by law by the respondent for eviction or exclusion of the aggrieved person from the shared household.
Thus, in appropriate case, the competent court can decide the claim in a properly instituted suit by the owner as to whether the women need to be excluded or evicted from the shared household.

One most common example for eviction and exclusion may be when the aggrieved person is provided same level of alternate accommodation or payment of rent as contemplated by Section 19 sub-section (f)
itself.
There may be cases where the plaintiff can successfully prove before the competent court that the claim of the plaintiff for eviction of the respondent is accepted.
We need not ponder for cases and circumstances where the eviction of exclusion can be allowed or refused.
It depends on facts of each case for which no further discussion is necessary in the facts of the present case.

The High Court in the impugned judgment has also expressed opinion that suit filed by the plaintiff cannot be held to be non-maintainable with which conclusion we are in agreement".
12.

The above ratio laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court makes it clear that in a suit filed by the parents-in-law against the daughter-in-law to claims to be an aggrieved person, the rights of both the parties shall be balanced and the civil court can pass suitable orders depending upon the facts of the each case.

In the light of the above legal position, court is required to examine present set of Suresh Kumar vs Chandan Shendge on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180413825/
6 facts.

13. Learned counsel appearing for the defendant No.2 has vehemently argued that defendant No.2 being a wife of defendant No.1 and as she had resided in the matrimonial home, she has a right of shared household and therefore the civil court cannot exclude her from matrimonial home.

It is contended by him that the burden of proving the domestic violence is on the plaintiffs and mere allegations of disturbance of peace and quarrels do not constitute civil injury or a domestic violence in the context of a civil injunction suit.

He has also argued that a direction for alternative accommodation would not address the core matrimonial issue which would defeat the matrimonial object of cohabitation as the husband would not accompany her and would continue to reside with the plaintiffs.
It is also contended by him that such an arrangement with artificially create physical separation between the spouses and push the marriage to permanent breakdown.

It is contended by him that permitting the wife to reside in the shared household with the husband promotes marital unity, accords with the statutory residence rights and avoid the civil court, becoming a vehicle to destroy the marriage and therefore allowing her to reside preserves the marital relationship rather than facilitating separation.
He has also contended that the very fact that a charge sheet is filed against the plaintiffs and defendant No.1 would prima-facie constitute the domestic violence against the plaintiffs.

He has also pointed out that defendant No.2 has already approached the Magistrate under Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, the Magistrate has taken cognizance of the complaint, issued notice to the plaintiffs, directed the CDPO to file the domestic incident report and granted a protection order in favour of defendant No.2 on 14.01.2006, which itself constitutes prima facie recognition of domestic violence and risk of harm and the matrimonial disputes are already under adjudication before the competent court and this court shall not grant the injunction in favour of the plaintiffs.

This Court has framed issue No.1 & 2 with regard to commission of domestic violence as there was no pending case before the Magistrate under the provisions of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005.

issued notice to the plaintiffs, directed the CDPO to file the Domestic Incident Report and granted a protection order in favour of defendant No.2 on 14.01.2026.

In the light of the subsequent developments, the Court would like to pass an order, which would be in force until the Magistrate passes suitable orders in the pending D.V. Act proceedings.
15. Earlier the plaintiffs have filed I.A.No.1 to restrain the defendants from interfering with their possession over the suit schedule property by way of temporary injunction.

This Court in the order dated 09.07.2024 after elaborately considering the scenario, granted an order of temporary injunction, restraining the defendants from interfering with the possession of the plaintiffs over the suit house during the pendency of the suit, reserving liberty to defendant No.2 to file an application under Section 19 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 against defendant No.1 for alternative accommodation or rent.

sentences.text: The said application is allowed by this Court in the order dated 08.10.2025, directing the defendant No.1 to pay a sum of 15,000/- per month as rent to enable the defendant No.2 to secure alternate accommodation during the pendency of the suit.
Therefore, the Court has made an attempt to protect the interest of both the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 during the pendency of the suit.

In the order passed by this Court in I.A.No.1 dated 09.07.2024, this Court has recorded reasons for granting an order of temporary injunction against defendants as hereunder:-
"As stated above the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 are in logger-heads from the inception, both pre-marriage and post-marriage of defendants 1 & 2.
Complaints and counter complaints have already been lodged and the records reveal that in the complaint filed by defendant No.2 investigation is also going on.

Under these circumstances, in the opinion of the court it would be appropriate to confirm the exparte order of temporary injunction already granted by this court reserving liberty to the defendant No.2 invoke her right of residence by filing an application under the relevant provisions of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 on the strength of Section 26 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, for the following reasons:
(1) The materials on record clearly indicates that the relationship of plaintiffs and defendant No.2 is completely strained even prior to the marriage and now in the complaint filed by defendant No.2 a criminal case is registered against the plaintiffs in Crime no.544/2023 of Hennur Police for the offences punishable under Section 498A, 341, 342, 323, 506 r/w/s 34 IPC and the case is under investigation.

(4) The plaintiff No.1 is a senior citizen.
The plaintiffs have contended that the plaintiff No.1 has suffered chest pain and unable to bear the stress and tension within the family.
Though the defendant No.2 has alleged domestic violence said to be committed by the plaintiff No.2 it appears that no direct overt act is attributed to the plaintiff No.1 who is a senior citizen.
The plaintiffs have contended that the defendant No.2 has even threatened that she would commit suicide.
Though the allegations and counter allegations are yet to be proved, it is improper to compel the plaintiffs to take the defendant No.2 under the circumstances of the case.
(5) It is admitted that suit house is a two bed room house and the plaintiffs are residing in it along with their 2nd son Akash Shindge and they have pleaded paucity space.
It is true that as rightly contended by the learned counsel appearing for the defendant No.2 earlier the defendant No.2 was accommodated in the same house.

But, for the purpose of convenience of the parties including defendant No.2 this is also a point that can be taken into consideration to decide as to whether alternative accommodation is more suitable to the defendant No.2 or she shall be permitted to reside in the suit premises.
The situation of the family during the time of good relationship is different when the relationship are strained.
Therefore, the defendant no.2 also suffer inconvenience to reside in the plaintiffs' house.

(6) In para-9 of the written statement, the defendant No.2 has pleaded that several instances initiated arguments between plaintiffs and defendant No.2 and in order to safeguard the relationship between plaintiffs and defendants, the defendant No.2 herself requested defendant No.1 for having a nuclear house during post marriage.

This stand taken by the defendant No.2 itself shows that she herself was not happy in the matrimonial home even prior to the marriage and therefore insisted the defendant No.1 to set up a separate house.

Such being the case, when the relationship is totally strained, it is improper to direct the parties to reside together rather directing defendant No.1 to provide alternative accommodation to the defendant No.2.
(7) The defendant No.2 has admitted that she is not with the plaintiffs in the suit house from October 2023.
It appears that she has not sought any separate relief under the provisions of Domestic Violence Act for shared house hold right even till today.
Their separation for about 9 months has created further gap in the relationship.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has made it clear that the right of residence u/s 19 is not an indefeasible right of residence to the aggrieved lady in the shared household especially when the daughter-in-law is pitted against aged father-in-law and mother-in-law and the senior citizens in the evening of their life are also entitled to live peacefully and not haunted by marital discord between their son and daughter-in-law.
This aspect is required to be seriously considered in the present case having regard to the nature of the dispute.
(9) The court is required to balance the rights of the parties.

In other words the provisions of Senior Citizens Act 2007 confers the right to the senior citizens and Section 19 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provides such a right to an aggrieved daughter-in-law and while passing the orders these two acts should be borne in mind to maintain balance between two warring parties and accordingly the conflict between the rights of the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 is required to be resolved.

16. After recording the above reasons, the plaintiffs as well as defendant No.2 have given evidence.

While the plaintiffs have taken up a contention that the defendant No.2 has harassed them and disturbed their peace during the evening of their life, the defendant No.2 has alleged domestic violence by the plaintiffs also along with her husband.

She has also produced several documents including the proceedings held in C.C.No.56094/2024, wherein a charge sheet is stated to be filed against the plaintiffs also for the offence punishable under Section 498-A and other alleged offences.

17. As stated above, when the plaintiff No.1 has claimed that he is a senior citizen and his rights are required to be protected and when the defendant No.2 contends domestic violence, Court is required to balance the rights of both the parties.

In the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Satish Chandra Ahuja v/s Neha Ahuja (2021)1 SCC 414 in para No.124, referred to above,
the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed that one most common example for eviction and exclusion of the aggrieved woman if she is provided same level of alternative accommodation or payment of rent as contemplated by Section 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

In order to protect the interest of defendant No.2, this court has already passed orders on I.A.No.8,
directing the defendant No.1 to pay rent of 15,000/- per month to enable the defendant No.2 to secure alternative level of accommodation.
Though a charge sheet is stated to be filed against the plaintiffs, it is too premature to record a finding as to whether the plaintiffs are guilty or not.
It is also necessary to note that apart from the DV Act proceedings, the divorce case is also pending before the Matrimonial Court.

Though the learned counsel appearing for defendant No.2 has vehementally contended that if the defendant No.2 is permitted to reside along with the plaintiffs in the matrimonial home, it will help for the reunion of the couple, the defendant No.2 has not produced any materials to show that the defendant No.1 is still residing in the suit schedule property along with the plaintiffs.
He has taken up a contention that he is residing separately.

Therefore,
unless there is a clear proof that the defendant No.1 is residing in the suit schedule property, no purpose would be served, even if the defendant No.2 is permitted to reside in the suit schedule house.
As stated above, it is rented house.

It is stated that it consists of only two rooms and the Suresh Kumar vs Chandan Shendge on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180413825/
10 plaintiffs as well as their another son is also residing in the same house.

In the course of orders passed by this court in I.A.No.1, this Court has made an observation that when the parties are in loggerhead and the relationship is strained as there are cases and counter cases, it is improper to lift the protection given to the plaintiffs.
18. The relationship of the parties are very sensitive.

In the opinion of the Court, when the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 are seriously contesting the litigations before the criminal court, D.V. Act court and matrimonial court, if the defendant No.2 is permitted to enter the suit schedule property, the possibilities of frequent quarrels and untoward incidents cannot be ruled out.
Admittedly, the defendant No.2 is employed and court has already passed an order directing the defendant No.1 to pay an amount of Rs.15,000/- per month to secure alternative level of accommodation.
The fate of the marital life will be decided only by the matrimonial court.

Though it is argued on behalf of the defendant No.2 is that if they were permitted to reside together, it will help for marital reunion, the family court will take care of the matter and the rights of the plaintiffs also cannot be ignored.

The learned Magistrate who is dealing with the D.V. Act proceedings is required to record a finding with regard to the domestic violence alleged by the defendant No.2 for other reliefs claimed by her.
The enquiry and finding by the D.V. Act Court is not limited to the question of shared household rights.
It will include maintenance, compensation, etc.

In view of these peculiar circumstances, if the defendants are prevented from interfering with the possession of the plaintiffs over the suit schedule property until suitable orders are passed by the DV Act court, it would serve the purpose.

If an order of injunction is not granted, the plaintiff No.1 being a senior citizen and plaintiff No.2 is also an aged lady, the consequences will be very serious and there is possibility of further clashes, additional litigations,
etc.

Under these circumstances, in the opinion of the court, issues No.1 & 2 does not arise consideration and issue No.3 is answered in the negative keeping open the question to be finally decided by the Court which has considered the matter under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.

But, the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 has conferred wide power to the Magistrate to deal with the situation and the Magistrate is armed with comprehensive powers for the implementation of the orders.
Though the civil court can also execute its own orders,
the powers conferred to a Magistrate under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act is Suresh Kumar vs Chandan Shendge on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180413825/
7 wider than the civil Court and effective implementations can be enforced by the Magistrate.
In the light of the subsequent developments, the Court would like to pass an order, which would be in force until the Magistrate passes suitable orders in the pending D.V. Act proceedings.
Subsequently, defendant No.2 has filed I.A.No.8 before this Court under Section 19 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 to direct the defendant No.1 to arrange alternative residential accommodation for the residence of defendant No.2.
Under these circumstances, in the opinion of the court it would be appropriate to confirm the exparte order of temporary injunction already granted by this court reserving liberty to the defendant No.2 invoke her right of residence by filing an application under the relevant provisions of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 on the strength of Section 26 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, for the following reasons:
(1) The materials on record clearly indicates that the relationship of plaintiffs and defendant No.2 is completely strained even prior to the marriage and now in the complaint filed by defendant No.2 a criminal case is registered against the plaintiffs in Crime no.544/2023 of Hennur Police for the offences punishable under Section 498A, 341, 342, 323, 506 r/w/s 34 IPC and the case is under investigation.

The situation of the family during the time of good relationship is different when the relationship are strained.
Such being the case, when the relationship is totally strained, it is improper to direct the parties to reside together rather directing defendant No.1 to provide alternative accommodation to the defendant No.2.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has made it clear that the right of residence u/s 19 is not an indefeasible right of residence to the aggrieved lady in the shared household especially when the daughter-in-law is pitted against aged father-in-law and mother-in-law and the senior citizens in the evening of their life are also entitled to live peacefully and not haunted by marital discord between their son and daughter-in-law.
In other words the provisions of Senior Citizens Act 2007 confers the right to the senior citizens and Section 19 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provides such a right to an aggrieved daughter-in-law and while passing the orders these two acts should be borne in mind to maintain balance between two warring parties and accordingly the conflict between the rights of the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 is required to be resolved.
In the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Satish Chandra Ahuja v/s Neha Ahuja (2021)1 SCC 414 in para No.124, referred to above,
the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed that one most common example for eviction and exclusion of the aggrieved woman if she is provided same level of alternative accommodation or payment of rent as contemplated by Section 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
Though the learned counsel appearing for defendant No.2 has vehementally contended that if the defendant No.2 is permitted to reside along with the plaintiffs in the matrimonial home, it will help for the reunion of the couple, the defendant No.2 has not produced any materials to show that the defendant No.1 is still residing in the suit schedule property along with the plaintiffs.
He has taken up a contention that he is residing separately.
Therefore,

In the opinion of the Court, when the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 are seriously contesting the litigations before the criminal court, D.V. Act court and matrimonial court, if the defendant No.2 is permitted to enter the suit schedule property, the possibilities of frequent quarrels and untoward incidents cannot be ruled out.
Having regard to these aspects, in the opinion of the court, when the D.V. Act Court has already taken cognizance of the matter, it is not proper to record any finding on issue No.1 & 2.
The reason is that in the present suit the question of domestic violence is required to be considered only to decide the shared household rights.
The learned Magistrate who is dealing with the D.V. Act proceedings is required to record a finding with regard to the domestic violence alleged by the defendant No.2 for other reliefs claimed by her.
The enquiry and finding by the D.V. Act Court is not limited to the question of shared household rights.
It will include maintenance, compensation, etc.
Therefore, if this Court records any finding on issue No.1 & 2, it will prejudice the rights of the parties and the possibilities of divergent opinion also cannot be ruled out.
In view of these peculiar circumstances, if the defendants are prevented from interfering with the possession of the plaintiffs over the suit schedule property until suitable orders are passed by the DV Act court, it would serve the purpose.
Further, the order passed in I.A.No.8 will be extended until the DV Act court passes suitable orders with regard to the shared household right of the defendant No.2.
